pr_title: varlink: add introspection support + varlinkctl + varlinkify one first command line tool (systemd-pcrextend)
pr_body:
This beefs up our Varlink game: it adds support for Varlink introspection to our codebase, i.e. this stuff: https://varlink.org/Service

Introspection matters as we make our Varlink services more accessible ourside of systemd.

A new tool "varlinkctl" is added for interfacing with Varlink services. It's really nice any easy to use, for example:

```console
$ varlinkctl info /run/systemd/resolve/io.systemd.Resolve
```

will introspect what the Varlink service behind the `/run/systemd/resolve/io.systemd.Resolve` socket provides. Equally nice:

```console
# varlinkctl info /usr/lib/systemd/systemd-pcrextend
```

to see what Varlink interfaces the specified binary offers.

This also adds some glue to make it very easy to add Varlink APIs to command line tools, and then does that to systemd-pcrextend, making an IPC API available that allows measuring arbitrary strings to a TPM2 PCR, with an event log record associated with it.
pr_comments: (there's a native python varlink module btw. given how trivial varlink actually is it's generally a better idea to use a native library for each language rather than wrapping systemd's C version)

I still find varlink annoying to pull in as a dep, it means I have to make sure it is packaged in all distributions, keep track of updates, it feels messy to require each tool to implement this independently. It would be much nicer if I just had to handle JSON and could leave the varlink bits to systemd. What would be much nicer is if systemd shipped a helper tool that does the varlink specific bits which then just calls the actual tool, passing the input as a JSON object on stdin. Then all I need is to parse JSON, which is much more trivial than having to do varlink stuff, which most people have never heard of.

Actually, thinking more about it, such a tool can be implemented independently anyway. Our tools can do varlink directly, and tools that can't do it directly could use such a wrapper tool to expose themselves over varlink. But such a wrapper tool can be added later

Then all I need is to parse JSON, which is much more trivial than having to do varlink stuff, which most people have never heard of.

varlink is just json, check the spec. it's *trivial* to reimplement: the method call ist just a json object followed by a single NUL byte, and the response is too. That is the whole protocol.

So if you just want to do json in mkosi, that's entirely fine, but you really don't need varlinkctl for that.

What varlinkctl gives you is introspection, syntax highlighting and stuff. But you don't need any of this for basic varlink.

issue_context.title: sd-varlink should implement `org.varlink.service.Get*()` methods
issue_context.body:
### Component

sd-varlink

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe

As discussed in #23785, one of the things to help get the testing automated is to have the `org.varlink.service.GetInfo()` and `org.varlink.service.GetInterfaceDescription()` methods implemented by services provided by `sd-varlink`.

According to the [varlink spec](https://varlink.org/Service) they should be implemented by every varlink service, but in systemd, for some reason, we chose to not implement them:

https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/f63d1b0efa64fe716c2855a0410ac47ad67f7dec/src/shared/varlink.c#L867-L870

This makes discovering interfaces/method quite difficult, as the only other method is to grep the sources directly, which is ugly and error prone.

Also, since ~2017, the `org.varlink.service.GetInterface()` method is called `GetInterfaceDescription()` [0], but we still match against the old name.

[0] https://github.com/varlink/libvarlink/commit/7f28847eae7571467c2cf63b7098e3b0082ca407

### Describe the solution you'd like

For example, the [org.varlink.resolver service](https://github.com/cherry-pick/com.redhat.resolver) implements these methods, which makes discovering interfaces/methods relatively easy:

```
# varlink info unix:///run/org.varlink.resolver
Vendor: Varlink
Product: Resolver
Version: 1
URL: https://github.com/varlink/org.varlink.resolver
Interfaces:
  com.redhat.resolver
  org.varlink.resolver
  org.varlink.service

# varlink call unix:///run/org.varlink.resolver/org.varlink.service.GetInfo   
{
  "interfaces": [
    "com.redhat.resolver",
    "org.varlink.resolver",
    "org.varlink.service"
  ],
  "product": "Resolver",
  "url": "https://github.com/varlink/org.varlink.resolver",
  "vendor": "Varlink",
  "version": "1"
}

# varlink call unix:///run/org.varlink.resolver/org.varlink.service.GetInterfaceDescription  '{ "interface": "org.varlink.resolver" }' | jq '.description' | sed 's/\\n/\n/g' 
"# Interface to resolve reverse-domain interface names to
# service adresses
interface org.varlink.resolver

# Get a list of all resolvable interfaces and information
# about the resolver's identity.
method GetInfo() -> (vendor: string, product: string, version: string, url: string, interfaces: []string)

# Resolve an interface name to a registered varlink service address
method Resolve(interface: string) -> (address: string)

error InterfaceNotFound (interface: string)
"
```

In this particular case, the `org.varlink.service.GetInterfaceDescription()` method just dumps the respective `.varlink` file:

```
# cat ~fsumsal/repos/com.redhat.resolver/src/org.varlink.resolver.varlink
# Interface to resolve reverse-domain interface names to
# service adresses
interface org.varlink.resolver

# Get a list of all resolvable interfaces and information
# about the resolver's identity.
method GetInfo() -> (
  vendor: string,
  product: string,
  version: string,
  url: string,
  interfaces: []string
)

# Resolve an interface name to a registered varlink service address
method Resolve(interface: string) -> (address: string)

error InterfaceNotFound (interface: string)
```

but since the format of the description field is not explicitly specified anywhere, it's up to a discussion, I guess (I'm not quite sure what's the sd-varlink's version of `.varlink` files).

/cc @evverx

### Describe alternatives you've considered

_No response_

### The systemd version you checked that didn't have the feature you are asking for

251
comments: We only use varlink internally so far, which meant introspection isn't really giving us much: if we are both the only provide and consumer of these interfaces then the interface description is not particularly relevant. This changes once we advertise these interfaces to other people though. In that case it might make sense to both export this information, and validate calls against the interface definitions.

>  if we are both the only provide and consumer of these interfaces then the interface description is not particularly relevant

Without that those interfaces can't be tested automatically and that's not ideal given that basically every PR changing anything triggers crashes, memory leaks, buffer overflows and stuff like that.

Having said that in terms of testing `systemd` it shouldn't be necessary to provide those methods. I think if it was possible to generate methods and their signatures using the source code it would suffice.

We can't do that, the C code is not descriptive enough to autogen signatures... So we have to encode the additional info currently not visible in the C code somehow and embedd it in the C code. And then to ensure that this doesn't get out of sync with the actual codepaths implemented, we should probably auto-validate each method call with this meta-info.

I don't think varlink should be promoted until it can be tested somehow then. There are three PRs at the moment where a half-baked perl script looking for `dispatch_table` and `varlink_server_bind_method_many` has managed to trigger a crash by just connecting to a socket, a memory leak by sending valid data and a global buffer-overflow by calling a valid method. It hasn't even stared fuzzing anything yet.

On top of that, I guess if we want to go with @keszybz's idea of exporting sd-varlink (https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/23785#issuecomment-1163160486) as a mean to test varlink services provided by systemd, the exported services/interfaces should then conform to the varlink spec (which would, in return, make them relatively easily test-able). So it looks like a win-win scenario.

shouldn't this check that _argv contains _command as the first item?

no. argv[0] can be anything, and that's fine. It's how multicall binaries are implemented and how execve() generally works. I see no reason why we need to be more restrictive here. I mean, we are already more restrictive by insisting that the argv[] array is not empty (there was a famous series of CVEs about that), but i don't think we need to check for more than that.
a generic comment here explaining what this module does would be useful, as it's a bit alien

This commit should be merged into the previous one

`field && field->field_type...`
same here, fields[] is an embedded array
is `symbol` guaranteed non-null here, or should the check be `symbol && *symbol`?
symbols[] is an embedded array, as mentioned elsewhere.
`symbol && *symbol`
symbols[] is an embedded array, hence checking for it being non-NULL doesn't really make sense.
assert or check `interface`
is field guaranteed non-null? `field && field->field_type...`
assert or check `p`
_VARLINK_FIELD_TYPE_END_MARKER is 0, how does this work?

fields[] is an embedded array of structs. The array is terminated with a struct initialized to all zeroes (i.e. `{}`). We defined `_VARLINK_FIELD_TYPE_END_MARKER` to zero, so that it will be implicitly set as field type on this last zero initialized struct. we use something similar on other places too.
PidRef?

not really necessary: it's our own child, hence we know exactly how long the pid is valid.

There might be value in eventually switching *everything* to PidRef, just as a matter of principle, but we aren't there yet, as safe_fork() will return you a pid_t, not a PidRef as of now.

Hence, there's not much a PidRef would gain us here for now, and would mean we'd have to do even more infrastructure work first, to teach safe_fork() PidRef and so on.

(and if we do that, then your sd-executor PR would probably be fucked up because exec_spawn() would also have to be updated to do PidRef
